en: The Fifty-third Chapter of the *Shi Dunlun Jizhuan Lunben* (The Collected Explanations of the Treatise by Shi Dunlun),
within the seventh of ten sections, explains the meaning of karma; that is, the definitive determination of the objects perceived by visual consciousness.
Among the mental factors associated with the ear-consciousness that takes visible form as its object, and among those associated with the mental consciousness,

volition (*cetanā*) may also be included in the definitive analysis of the volition-numerical category associated with the assistants of those six consciousnesses, because they all possess the nature of karma.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the explanation of the three natures and the three types of karma;
second, the explanation of the three types of karma, such as non-restraint (*asaṃvara*).
In the preceding section,
the first part distinguishes the characteristics of karma,
while the latter clarifies its provisional and substantial natures.
Furthermore, what is manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*)? Briefly stated, there are three kinds.
Regarding the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), Jing (Jingxiu) and Buque (Fajing) state:
Among these three types of informative action (*vijñapti-karman*), regarding the two actions of body and speech:

if their essential nature is defined according to their specific characteristics, they consist of matter and sound produced by the transformation of volition (*cetanā*) of the three moral natures; these constitute the essential nature of bodily and vocal action.
Regarding that mental action (*manas-karman*): the fundamental volition (*cetanā*) that arises simultaneously with the body and speech is the essence of mental action.

If one sets aside its objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) and extracts its essential nature from the perspective of its manifestation, then that fundamental volition, relying upon the gateways of body and speech, is termed bodily and vocal informative action (*vijñapti-karman*).
The preliminary application of volition is called the informative action of the mind.
Regarding non-informative action:
within the desire realm, the essence of the three types of action—wholesome or unwholesome—is established either according to the aspect of the object or according to the manifestation of the view.

The seeds perfumed by that karma, within this continuum of seeds, prevent the occurrence of the wholesome by the unwholesome and the unwholesome by the wholesome; thus, "manifest activity" is a conventional designation.
As long as the intended period has not yet expired, these karmic seeds increase with every moment; this is called the "accomplishment of karma."
If the momentum is exhausted or the aspiration ceases such that the seeds of karma no longer increase, this is termed the "abandonment of karma.

As for the sevenfold non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) associated with the path of meditative concentration and the precepts, it is established based on the meaning of a single moment of volition (*cetanā*) and mental engagement (*manas*) as they actually arise.

Because a single thought-moment can abandon the sevenfold transgressions, and because the teachings of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna state that the precepts of the path and meditative concentration arise and cease according to the mind and do not continue in a constant stream.
If one were to establish the precepts of the path based on seeds, they would be constantly continuous; thus, it could not be said that they "arise and cease according to the mind."

The bodhisattva’s pure precepts—whether expressed through body, speech, or mind—are defined, as previously stated, either by way of their objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) or their subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*).

If they are unmanifest karma (*avijñapti-karma*), they consist in the seed of that karma which, following the original vow, increases more and more from the moment of its initial undertaking until the attainment of enlightenment.
Next, I shall explain its name.
The body and speech of the manifested form have as their essence visible matter and sound.
When arising from activity, it expresses matters such as intention, joy, or anger; thus,
the *nimittabhāga* (image-part) manifests the *darśanabhāga* (seeing-part),
which is also termed "manifesting the essence by means of the image."
Thus, the *Śata-śāstra* says:
"It is like a fish in a hidden current;
by stirring the waves, it reveals itself."
Mental informative action cannot be manifested to others;
it merely manifests its own perceived object.
Now, it is said that bodily and vocal informative karma (vijñapti-karma) are named after that which they represent—namely, the body and speech;
whereas mental informative karma is caused by its association with the cognition of objects.
As for non-informative karma (avijñapti-karma):
There are two meanings [to this].
First, with respect to the manifest body and speech, that which indicates their nature according to whether they are wholesome or unwholesome is called "manifest action" (*vijñapti-karma*).
If, in relation to a different nature, it cannot indicate [that nature], it is also called "non-manifest" (*avijñapti*).
Just as virtue does not manifest non-virtue and non-virtue does not manifest virtue,
and so forth— secondly, regarding the categories of bodily and vocal karma,
that which is conventionally designated as having the nature of karma but cannot manifest matters such as virtue or non-virtue is called "unmanifest" (avijñapti).
The path, discipline, and ritual regulations arise and cease in dependence upon the mind;
because they cannot represent anything according to external objects, they are called non-informative action (*avijñapti-karman*).
Herein, however, only informative action (*vijñapti-karman*) is discussed.
Briefly stated, there must be a reason why the principle of non-manifest action (*avijñapti*) does not apply here; it is because [the mind] possesses seeds.
Regarding mental manifest action (*manovijñapti-karman*):
if one regards it as that which makes its own object known, it is designated by the name "manifest action," which refers to its functional capacity.

The natures of the wholesome and the unwholesome are distinct: the wholesome does not substitute for the unwholesome, yet there is that which is manifested; the unwholesome does not substitute for the wholesome, yet there is likewise that which is manifested, which is also termed "unmanifest" (*avijñapti*).
This is established from the perspective of the seeds (*bīja*).
Regarding non-informative action (*avijñapti-karman*):
although it is provisionally established as a manifestation based on seeds, it cannot manifest or represent any object;
therefore, it is called mental non-informative action (*mānasy-avijñapti*).

Following this, after the explanation of the two unconditioned phenomena, space and so forth, at the end of this fascicle, he concludes by stating:

Judging by the flow of the text, this serves as a concluding summary of everything from the fifty-second [section] onward;
the "seeds" at the end of the previous fascicle and the "karma" mentioned here are all responses to latent objections.

Karma is established based upon the seeds;

thereby resolving the meaning of the eight paths of action (*karmapatha*) from the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (the "Root" in eight fascicles).

Regarding the statement, "If [one engages] in the ten unwholesome paths of action of body, speech, and mind,
etc.," Jing says:
The first seven are both karma and paths;
the latter three—greed, hatred, and wrong view—are paths but not karma.
Why, then, is it said here that the three karmas of body, speech, and mind are called the ten unwholesome courses of action?
The commentary explains:
This statement is made based on the fact that mental karma is simultaneously associated with greed, hatred, and wrong view;
therefore, it refers to the ten unwholesome paths of action of body, speech, and mind.
The path of mental intention (*manas-karman*) is not the latter three paths,
because mental intention is an action (*karman*) rather than a path (*mārga*).
As for "not being separate":
"Those seeds of karma follow [the person] without ever departing.
Regarding "due to the predominant power of the manifest activity," this means that by virtue of the predominant power of those seeds in relation to that manifest activity.
It gives rise to all defiled manifest actions (*vijñapti-karman*) of body and speech;
the full text states:
"not yet free from that which is to be countered by the Noble Path (*ārya-mārga*)."
Therefore, it is said that they are not separate.
My current interpretation differs slightly:
the following clarifies that within the context of wholesome karma, one vows to maintain distance from them.
Therefore, one should know that this statement "not separated from active manifestation" means not being separated from the ten unwholesome actions. If these very [actions],
when brought to their culmination, are designated as wholesome manifest karma, [then so it is].
Jingyun: Since it is said that one vows to undertake the abstention from the manifest karma of body and speech,
this refers to the mere volition and aspiration that have not yet given rise to physical or vocal action.
How is it that they are called bodily and vocal informative karma (*kāya-vāk-vijñapti-karman*)?
The explanation says:
if one bases this on the performance of wholesome deeds.
At that time, there are no two types of karma— bodily and verbal.
However, according to the perspective of virtuous restraint (*saṃvara*),
they do exist at that time.
Because at the time of undertaking the vow,
within a single mental volition there is an abstention from the seven non-virtuous actions of body and speech,
this mental volition is designated as "wholesome karma of body and speech."
Therefore, there is no fault.

This follows the Sarvāstivāda doctrine of "concomitant transformation" (anuvartaka).

Now, this Mahāyāna [teaching] applies to all three natures (trisvabhāva).

excluding the wholesome and the unwholesome.

This refutes the Hīnayāna attachment to the notion that bodily action (*kāyakarman*) in a single moment has motion as its actual substance;
rather, it is established that, based on a continuum where this ceases and that arises, "bodily action" is merely a conventional designation.
Because there is no movement in a single thought-moment, there is no real karma.
This is stated with respect to the objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga) of the fundamental consciousness (mūla-vijñāna), wherein the sense-faculties and matter cease here and arise there,
in order to refute the attachments of outsiders.

Paramārtha says:

"The masters of the Saṃmitīya school maintain that within the continuity of material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) throughout a single lifetime, there is a distinct movement of the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), which is called bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*)."
Now, its refutation is stated as follows:
Moment by moment, there is a continuous succession of arising and ceasing; it ceases at this location and arises at another.
It is not the case that within a single, substantial entity there is no arising or ceasing, such that it could proceed to another place without ceasing here.
In the Vaiśeṣika categories, extension, contraction, and so forth likewise possess substantial reality;
now, these are refuted in the same manner.
Even according to the Sarvāstivādins, although there is no "moving color" (gati-rūpa), there exists a distinct "action-color" (karma-rūpa).
Just as when bending or extending [a limb], there arises a distinct material form (*rūpa*) produced by karma,
it is not so here. Rather,
it is only the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) material body of maturation (*vipāka*) that, through the power of volition (*cetanā*), undergoes transformation and arises in this place.
Since there is no separate substantial entity of matter (rūpa) that constitutes karma,
it is said that "only the body perishes in other locations," and so forth. Furthermore,
it is only the vocal sound itself that is designated as the informative action of speech (vāgvijñapti-karman).
This distinguishes [the position] from that of the Sarvāstivādins, for whom sound is itself vocal action (*vāk-karman*).
Here, it is stated that there is only vocal sound;
that which is produced by the action of volition (*cetanā-karman*) is called vocal manifest action (*vāk-vijñapti-karman*), and its essence is exclusively neutral (*avyākṛta*).
Unlike the Hīnayāna, where the substance of karma (*karmabhāva*) pervades all three moral natures (*trividha-svabhāva*),
[in this system] only the volition (*cetanā*) that initiates the mind and performs an action is called "informative mental karma" (*manas-karman-vijñapti*).
This statement takes *cetanā* to be the mental karma.
Mental karma also initiates bodily and vocal actions, taking volition as its activity.
Karma is indeed form, yet it is a conventional designation;
there is no separate form that is called "karma" and so forth.
As for the phrase "Why? Because it is not even logically tenable," this refutes the Saṃmitīya school and others;
one must first establish that [the entity] possesses momentariness.
Only then can one refute the [position that] there is no motion.
One should first establish the following formal argument (*pramāṇa*):
"All material objects (*rūpa*) and so forth must perish moment by moment."
Because they are subsumed within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*),
like the flame of a lamp and the sound of a bell;
for the flame of a lamp and the sound of a bell are commonly accepted by others.
He then establishes the formal argument (prayoga), saying:
"There is no such visible form that travels to another location,
because it perishes moment by moment."
Just as in the case of a lamp flame and so forth,
this cause for momentary destruction is what is fully established.
Furthermore, apart from the mere arising of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), no other real activity can be perceived by the eye, the ear, or the mind.

and it also refutes the Vaiśeṣika school’s [view of] the real nature of the category of action (karma-pada).
Now, in general, it is denied as follows:
there is no distinct, real activity,
for the three types of action apprehended by the eye, the ear, and the mind are all unfindable.

Your claim that the karma of movement (*gati-karma*) and so forth exists as a form (*rūpa*) distinct from all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is untenable, because it cannot be apprehended by the eye, the ear, or the mind.

The text is divided into four parts.

whereas the non-virtuous restraint is called a path of action only when it arises in the midst of its actual occurrence?
The Tripiṭaka master says:
Because the restraint of the virtuous discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*) is itself wholesome, it constitutes a path of action (*karmapatha*).
Jing says:
"The essential nature of the non-virtuous discipline consists of the ten unwholesome paths of action as well as evil intentions and vows."
Its essence consists of constant association with lack of faith, laziness, false mindfulness, distraction, and unwholesome wisdom.

if regarding this matter of livelihood one again gives rise to a mind of desire, pleasure, or acceptance,

"Because it is comprised within non-restraint," and so forth.
According to the Tripiṭaka Master,

Based on the presence of the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*), the state of grossness (*dausthulya*), and the lack of functional flexibility (*akarmanyatā*),
these exist within the retribution of the first dhyāna;
it is only upon attaining the second meditative absorption (*dvitīya-dhyāna*) that one is finally freed from them.
In the first dhyāna, the coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*) of the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) is different [from that below].
According to the *Abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*, the first dhyāna still possesses three types of consciousness;
because it serves as the basis for the faculty of suffering, it is said to "possess the faculty of suffering."
Regarding the distinctions within the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), Ki states:
"As for the distinctions among inversions, it refers to the fact that all foolish worldlings lack understanding, and so forth, up to what is called 'inversion of perception' (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*)."
Regarding ignorance (*avidyā*):
as stated in the eighth [chapter], it is the root of these inversions.
Here, according to its characteristics, it is a number.
However, if the distortions arising internally and externally are collectively termed "distortions of perception" (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*),
they are further divided therein into "distortions of mind" (*citta-viparyāsa*) and "distortions of view" (*dṛṣṭi-viparyāsa*).
If those who have gone forth as non-Buddhist ascetics give rise to three views in their entirety, or one part or a small portion thereof, in conjunction with perception;
This is a perversion of view and also a perversion of perception.
If a householder gives rise to craving toward an object, it is accompanied by a perversion of perception;
it is called a perversion of perception and is also a perversion of mind.
However, the eighth fascicle of the first volume previously stated:
"Greed comprises two types: namely, the inversion of the impure as pure, and the inversion of suffering as pleasure;

furthermore, it includes the grasping at wrong precepts and wrong views by non-Buddhists during their practice, such as the attachment to views regarding precepts and the pursuit of rebirth in heaven."
Because this craving is predominant, these two alone are specifically designated as the "perverted minds of craving.
Other [perversions], such as the views of self and permanence, are not mentioned here because their meanings are common to all sentient beings and thus remain implicit.
If one follows this text,
the arising of the inversion of permanence and self in external worldlings is also an inversion of mind;
thus, the inversion of mind applies to both the lay and monastic communities.

However, in this present text, the term "inversion of mind" (*cittaviparyāsa*) is used as a general designation for those householders who give rise to inversions regarding the objects of desire, because their greed is predominant;
whereas the term "inversion of view" (*dṛṣṭiviparyāsa*) is used for non-Buddhists, because the activity of their views is predominant.
However, one cannot say that the inversion of views arises among the householders;
therefore, this differs from the preceding eight passages.
Furthermore, another interpretation states:
In this passage from the *Gṛhastha-varga*, it is stated that the mind gives rise to a perversion regarding the permanent self (*nityātman*).
However, since non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) also conceive of a permanent self,
[the text] mentions it because they share this conception.
The preceding text states only that the inversions of pleasure (*sukha*) and purity (*śubha*) arise within the category of householders; however,
since the inversions of permanence (*nitya*) and self (*ātman*) apply to both the categories of householders and renunciants,
one cannot say that [the latter two] arise only among householders.
The meaning of greed is further explained as "perversion of mind" (*cittaviparyāsa*).
Thus, it is the same as this text’s statement that householders give rise to perversion of mind while those who have left the home life give rise to perversion of view (*dṛṣṭiviparyāsa*);
the former interpretation is superior.
However, judging by the principles of the doctrine:
it may be possible for a layperson not to give rise to the inversion of views, but for one who has left the household life,
it is impossible not to give rise to the inversion of craving.
Because false desire, the precepts and views, and the two types of grasping are considered causes for rebirth in heaven or for liberation;
if one explains it in this way,
the perversion of perception (saṃjñā-viparyāsa) is understood to be abandoned through both seeing and cultivation, as it serves as the basis for the two perversions of mind and view.
The inversion of view arises only in the Path of Seeing,
because it is produced by those who have gone forth as non-Buddhist outsiders;
whereas the inversion of mind occurs throughout both the categories of householders and those who have gone forth.
It is abandoned through both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation;
furthermore, it arises solely from conceptual discrimination abandoned by the path of seeing.
Cè states:
According to the *Foxing lun* (Treatise on the Buddha-nature), that is called the perversion of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*);
the internal [perversion] is called the perversion of view (*dṛṣṭi-viparyāsa*); and that of the mind is called the perversion of mind (*citta-viparyāsa*).
Now, according to this treatise,
that which is associated with the four inversions is called "inversion of perception" (saṃjñā-viparyāsa).
The wisdom that reckons [things] as permanent and so forth is called the inversion of view;
craving is called the inversion of mind. Buque says:
As for "a portion of those who have left the household life":
because they have left the household life within the Buddha-dharma,
they are designated as "outsiders" (tīrthika) and thus termed "a portion of those who have left the household life."
T'ai says:
"To be able to discern all objects is called 'equal discernment' (samprajanya).
Furthermore, to be able to discern those dharmas is also called 'equal discernment'."
The section on the initial gate of the intrinsic nature of the five marks of conditioned activity is concluded.
